subtitle: Learn clear, plain-language distinctions between representation, participation, equity, access and intercultural learning. You can then use each term well in everyday work.
scope: For staff across DHS who want to understand the terms used in People, Access and Culture work and connect them to a concrete task. This is a learning glossary with practice cases, not a legal finding, accommodation decision, cultural assessment or certification of required training. Required policies and authorized procedures remain separate.
introTranscript: A useful term helps people understand a decision; an unexplained term can hide the question. This course gives common equity, inclusion and accessibility words a concrete meaning through a team in this example reviewing a service meeting and its materials. You will distinguish who is present from whose knowledge influences the work, a result from its explanation, a general access barrier from an individual employment accommodation, and cultural awareness from adapted practice. You will also turn a broad statement into a clear work question with an appropriate next step. The aim is to use the words accurately without labeling colleagues or making people disclose personal information.

lessons.summary: Connect a broad DEIA term to a concrete work question.
lessons.objective: Explain DEIA as four related areas of attention.
objectives: Explain DEIA as four related areas of attention.
Identify which part of a practice task an unfamiliar term concerns.
Rewrite a broad statement as a question that can be examined.
takeaways: A term needs context to become useful.
Different terms can describe different parts of the same task.
Ask for clarification without treating the question as resistance.
lessons.statement: Name the work question before relying on the label.

intro.heading: The words should make the work clearer
intro.body:
DEIA is a common abbreviation for diversity, equity, inclusion and accessibility. These areas connect, but they do not answer exactly the same question. A diverse group may be present without its knowledge influencing a decision. A clear invitation may still be inaccessible. A useful improvement may affect one barrier while leaving another unresolved. The words become helpful when staff explain the particular part of the work they mean.

Consider a DHS team reviewing a service meeting. A colleague says the meeting should be more inclusive. That statement identifies a worthwhile concern but not yet a specific change. Does the concern involve who was invited, whether the agenda was understandable, how people could contribute, or whether their input reached the decision? Several of those conditions may matter, and they need different evidence.

Clarifying the term should make participation easier rather than test a colleague’s knowledge. A respectful question might ask which part of the meeting needs attention and what happened in that part. Do not assume that someone who requests a definition opposes the purpose. Staff can understand the subject well while using different words or needing the process explained.

This course uses DHS definitions where they apply and explains working examples in ordinary language. A definition helps organize thought; it does not decide an actual legal matter or authorize a process change. Keep a named policy requirement accurate and use its responsible procedure when needed. For a general learning question, identify the task, the concern and the evidence or next step that would help. The following lessons build the distinctions so the team can move beyond a positive label to a specific, reviewable improvement.

inThisLesson: Identify the task behind the term.
lessons.keyStatement: Clear terminology supports understanding; it should not become an access gate.

flashcards.back: Diversity, equity, inclusion and accessibility: related concerns about people, opportunity, participation and usable access.
The task, decision or situation in which a word is being used.
A specific issue that can be examined through evidence and relevant perspectives.
A request to understand meaning, not proof of disagreement or lack of commitment.

items.title: Specific meaning
items.body: Ask what part of the meeting the word inclusive describes. An invitation list and an opportunity to influence a draft are different parts of the process. Naming the part makes the concern actionable without requiring a long glossary discussion.

items.title: Different understandings
items.body: People may use one word for different experiences. Summarize what you heard and invite correction instead of arguing over who used the word first. The task and effect matter more than displaying technical vocabulary.

items.title: Named requirements
items.body: A formal policy term may carry responsibilities that a general definition does not capture. Preserve the actual requirement and consult its procedure. A learning explanation should not replace a legal definition or a responsible office’s decision.

tabs.label: Positive label
tabs.body: “The meeting is inclusive” expresses a conclusion without the supporting account. Ask who could participate, how input was considered and what remains unknown. The label alone is not evidence of everyone’s experience.

tabs.label: Concrete question
tabs.body: “Could written questions reach the person deciding before the choice closed?” identifies a participation condition. It can be checked without asking staff to disclose identity or defend an ideological position.

tabs.label: Vocabulary test
tabs.body: Requiring people to define every term before they contribute creates an unnecessary barrier. Explain the relevant word and examine the concern. A question about terminology can improve shared understanding.

check.question: What is the most useful response to “make the meeting more inclusive”?
check.correct: Ask which participation condition needs attention and what evidence or experience identifies it.
wrong: Treat the phrase as proof that every process is failing.
Require a terminology examination before receiving input.
check.feedbackCorrect: The question connects the label to a specific condition that can be examined respectfully.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A broad phrase does not establish every finding or motive. A vocabulary gate also does not improve access to the work. Clarify the task, concern and supporting account before deciding the response.

items.text: Inclusion concerns whether relevant contributions can matter in the meeting.
Accessibility concerns whether materials and participation methods can be used.
Did written questions reach the person authorized to decide?
Which material could not be opened or understood?
Asking for a definition proves resistance.
The word inclusive proves every participant felt included.

scenario.context: DHS practice case: A staff member asks what inclusion means for a service-review meeting. A colleague calls the question resistance.
options: Explain the relevant participation question and invite the concern.
Require the staff member to prove personal commitment.
Avoid the topic because the words are disputed.
responses: Clarification helps the group examine the actual work without judging motive.
The demand shifts attention away from the useful question.
Avoidance leaves the work concern unresolved.

lessons.transfer: Turn a broad DEIA statement into a task, a concern and a question that can be examined.

move.control: You can explain the relevant term and invite a practical question.
move.failure: Vocabulary becomes a label for people or a substitute for evidence.
move.next: Write a concrete question about the practice meeting.

lessons.title: Distinguish who is present from whose contribution matters
lessons.summary: Explain diversity and inclusion through representation and participation.
lessons.objective: Distinguish diversity from inclusion in a practice meeting.
objectives: Distinguish diversity from inclusion in a practice meeting.
Identify a participation condition that attendance alone cannot show.
Describe evidence that input informed a changed or unchanged choice.
takeaways: Diversity concerns differences among people and perspectives.
Inclusion concerns valued participation and belonging, not attendance alone.
A contribution can inform a decision without guaranteeing the preferred choice.
lessons.statement: Representation and influence need separate questions.

image.caption: Two colleagues point to a line in a printed document they are reviewing together.

intro.heading: Presence does not tell the whole story
intro.body:
Diversity concerns differences among people and groups. DHS’s policy describes those differences broadly; they include more than a single visible identity category. Inclusion concerns the value of contributions and people’s sense of belonging. Representation can bring relevant perspectives into a room, but attendance alone cannot establish that those perspectives were heard, considered or able to influence the work.

In the practice service meeting, participants include people with different work roles, languages and experiences. The team can accurately describe that range if the information is appropriately available. But the agenda gives only senior staff time to speak, and written concerns are reviewed after the decision is finalized. That process may prevent relevant knowledge from reaching the choice even though the attendance list looks varied.

Ask how the contribution route works: when materials arrive, which response methods are usable, who considers the input and what can still change. Do not require participants to tell personal stories or represent a whole identity group. A staff member can offer a specific service-design concern without becoming the spokesperson for every person who shares an identity.

Inclusion also does not mean every idea must be adopted or every disagreement removed. Input may improve an option, support an unchanged choice or identify a condition the team cannot yet resolve. Explain the reason and follow-through. A respectful account of influence is more informative than a promise of universal satisfaction. Use attendance as one piece of process evidence and examine participation and influence separately. Those distinctions help the team identify the improvement it can actually make without assuming everyone’s experience from a list.

inThisLesson: Record how input influenced the choice.
lessons.keyStatement: A participant’s presence is not a complete account of participation or belonging.

flashcards.back: The presence of differences among people and groups, including relevant experiences and perspectives.
Valued contribution and belonging; it requires attention to participation, not merely a head count.
Who is present or included in a described group.
How relevant input can affect the decision, including its reasons and unresolved questions.

items.title: Preparation
items.body: Materials provided early enough for the actual task can make a contribution more useful. Check whether people had the relevant information rather than treat a delayed question as unwillingness. Preparation is a process condition, not a measure of personal confidence.

items.title: Response routes
items.body: Written, verbal or supported methods can help different people contribute. Their usefulness depends on whether the input reaches the decision in time. Offering a route that no one reviews can produce activity without influence.

items.title: Reasons
items.body: Explain what the input supported and why a choice changed or remained unchanged. A reasoned decision can retain disagreement. Do not claim that attendance, a smile or the absence of complaints establishes that everyone belongs.

tabs.label: Attendance list
tabs.body: The list may establish who attended, if appropriately recorded. It cannot explain whether the agenda allowed meaningful contribution or how people experienced the process. Do not turn the list into a personal disclosure requirement.

tabs.label: Input record
tabs.body: A bounded record can show which question was considered, what evidence was checked and how the answer affected the decision. Protect information and avoid including unnecessary personal histories.

tabs.label: Satisfaction claim
tabs.body: A claim that everyone was satisfied needs evidence beyond a completed meeting. People can contribute while remaining dissatisfied. Describe the process and known results without declaring an experience for every participant.

check.question: What evidence is most useful for the practice inclusion question?
check.correct: Whether relevant input could reach the choice in time and how it informed the decision.
wrong: A rule requiring every participant to speak for an identity group.
Proof of agreement with every proposed idea.
check.feedbackCorrect: This examines participation and influence rather than replacing them with representation or forced consensus.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Attendance is relevant but limited. Group representation demands and universal agreement requirements can create barriers. Trace the contribution through preparation, response and decision, then explain its actual influence.

items.text: Different work roles attended the practice meeting.
The team invited people affected by the service proposal.
A written question reached the person deciding before finalization.
The decision record explains why an option remained unchanged after input.
A varied room proves everyone felt included.
Inclusion requires every idea to be adopted.

lessons.next: Next, distinguish an observed difference from an inequity conclusion.

scenario.context: DHS practice case: The meeting has a varied attendance list but only senior voices can reach the draft before it is finalized.
options: The contribution conditions and decision influence, alongside representation.
Which participants should be required to tell personal stories.
Whether a positive group photograph can replace a process review.
responses: This identifies the gap between presence and usable participation.
Personal disclosure is not the missing decision route.
A photograph cannot establish how the process worked.

lessons.transfer: Describe one representation detail, one participation condition and one limit on what they can establish.

move.control: You can make the contribution route and reasons clearer.
move.failure: A varied group is mistaken for complete inclusion.
move.next: Trace one practice question from invitation to decision.

lessons.title: Distinguish equity, differences and inequities
lessons.summary: Use evidence carefully when describing access or outcome differences.
lessons.objective: Explain equity as ongoing attention and action concerning access, opportunity and outcomes.
objectives: Explain equity as ongoing attention and action concerning access, opportunity and outcomes.
Distinguish a recorded difference from a supported conclusion about inequity.
Identify evidence needed before explaining a group pattern.
takeaways: A difference is an observation, not a complete explanation.
Inequity concerns a systematic, avoidable and unjust difference.
An equity response needs evidence, affected perspectives and follow-through.
lessons.statement: State what the evidence shows before explaining why it happened.

image.caption: Two colleagues point to a line in a printed document they are reviewing together.

intro.heading: Terms should preserve the limits of evidence
intro.body:
Equity is an ongoing practice of examining and addressing barriers, power, access, opportunities and outcomes. It is not established by a favorable label or a single activity count. DHS defines inequities as differences in outcomes that are systematic, avoidable and unjust. Those features require an examination of the pattern and its context. A recorded difference alone does not supply the entire explanation.

In the practice meeting review, one unit received the appendix before the discussion while another received it afterward. That is a documented preparation difference. The team can investigate whether the handoff created a preventable disadvantage in participation. It should not immediately infer a person’s motive or declare that every outcome difference between the units has the same cause.

DHS’s policy also uses disparity in a specific way: systematic poorer outcomes not explained by the group’s needs, eligibility or preferences. A course exercise can help identify an evidence question, but it cannot establish those conditions by subtracting two rates. Use the actual policy meaning when making a formal claim and distinguish it from a descriptive difference in a practice example.

A useful response asks what the process does, who bears its burdens, what affected perspectives identify and which evidence supports an explanation. Some questions may remain unresolved because information is missing, unsuitable or not authorized for that use. Record the limit instead of inventing a reassuring conclusion. Equity work can begin with a supported concern and a responsible next step while fuller analysis continues. Keep the language proportionate to the evidence and avoid treating a group label as the cause of a pattern.

inThisLesson: Identify what a formal claim would need.
lessons.keyStatement: A supported observation can begin the inquiry without completing its explanation.

flashcards.back: Ongoing action concerning barriers, power, access, opportunity and outcomes.
A descriptive observation that two recorded conditions or results are not the same.
An outcome difference examined as systematic, avoidable and unjust, using the relevant context and evidence.
A statement of what available information cannot establish.

items.title: Observation
items.body: State who received the practice appendix and when. That is more useful than immediately labeling a colleague unfair. The handoff can be checked and changed through appropriate authority without claiming a complete explanation for all participation patterns.

items.title: Context
items.body: Examine the decision point, preparation needs and other relevant conditions. A late appendix may affect one issue while another concern has a different explanation. Do not combine distinct problems into an unsupported single cause.

items.title: Missing information
items.body: If authorized evidence is not available, name the gap. Missing data are not zero problems, and a completed course is not an outcome measure. A clear inquiry can identify the evidence and responsible review needed next.

tabs.label: Descriptive difference
tabs.body: “The second unit received the appendix after the decision” states an observed process fact in the practice case. It supports a handoff review without establishing every legal or equity finding.

tabs.label: Supported concern
tabs.body: “The late handoff may have prevented relevant questions from informing the draft” identifies a plausible concern to investigate. Examine the timeline and participants’ task accounts before reporting it as the established cause.

tabs.label: Automatic conclusion
tabs.body: “That unit’s identity explains its lower participation” substitutes a label for evidence. A group category does not tell the team why the contribution route worked differently. Return to the process and supporting information.

check.question: What is the most accurate description of the practice handoff?
check.correct: A recorded preparation difference that may create a barrier and needs context and evidence before a broader conclusion.
wrong: Proof that every difference is unjust.
Reassurance that no issue exists because the appendix was eventually sent.
check.feedbackCorrect: The statement uses the observation to form a useful inquiry while keeping cause, intent and wider conclusions open.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A single difference does not establish every feature of inequity or anyone’s motive. Eventual distribution also may not repair lost influence before a decision. Describe timing, task effect and the evidence needed next.

items.text: One unit received the appendix after finalization.
The practice invitation routes had different preparation windows.
Did the late handoff prevent a relevant question from being considered?
What authorized information supports a broader pattern?
The group label caused the difference.
Missing information proves there were no barriers.

lessons.next: Next, distinguish general accessibility from an individual employment accommodation.

scenario.context: DHS practice case: Staff observe different contribution rates and want to call the cause proven without checking the preparation conditions.
options: Report the observation, examine the context and name the evidence needed for an explanation.
Choose a cultural explanation without new evidence.
Delete the figures because uncertainty remains.
responses: This makes the observation useful while avoiding unsupported cause or identity claims.
A new stereotype is not a source-grounded explanation.
Uncertainty can be stated honestly while appropriate inquiry continues.

lessons.transfer: Write one observed difference, one possible process explanation and one evidence limit.

move.control: You can use accurate terms and preserve uncertainty.
move.failure: An observation becomes a finding that the available evidence cannot support.
move.next: Describe the practice handoff and the next inquiry without assigning motive.

lessons.title: Distinguish accessibility from an employment accommodation
lessons.summary: Identify the setting and relevant response without making every access concern the same process.
lessons.objective: Distinguish a general material-access barrier from an individual employment accommodation request.
objectives: Distinguish a general material-access barrier from an individual employment accommodation request.
Identify why effective communication depends on the task and the person’s method.
Choose the relevant authorized route without collecting unnecessary medical information.
takeaways: Accessibility examines whether environments, materials and methods can be used.
Employment accommodations have an individual authorized process.
One improved format does not establish every communication need is met.
lessons.statement: Locate the setting and need before deciding which process applies.

image.caption: Two colleagues point to a line in a printed document they are reviewing together.

intro.heading: Access is connected to the actual task
intro.body:
Accessibility concerns whether people can use an environment, material, service or participation method. It can be considered in planning for a broad audience, such as preparing an understandable, usable meeting packet. An employment accommodation is an individual adjustment under the applicable workplace process for a qualified applicant or employee with a disability. The ideas connect, but their settings and procedures should not be merged automatically.

In the practice team, a public meeting packet contains an image of text that cannot be used in the relevant screen-reader test. The team should use the responsible material-access process to address the document and communication task. Separately, an employee requests a change in how a training is provided because of a medical condition. That request needs the employment accommodation route; the team should not assume that fixing the public packet resolves it.

For covered public-service communication, the task’s nature, length, complexity and context, and the person’s normal communication method matter. Large print, accessible electronic text, captioning or an interpreter may address different needs. Do not assign an aid solely from a category such as deaf or blind, or assume that any written note is sufficient for every complex exchange. Coordinate the appropriate qualified help through applicable procedures.

Under Policy 1433, an employment request can begin without special terminology. The person receiving it promptly forwards it to the appropriate decision maker and explains who that is. Supervisors and managers must not request medical information or documentation; any appropriate request belongs to the ADA Coordinator. Agencies must not request or accept medical records. These boundaries protect the process. Staff can identify the task issue and appropriate route without diagnosing a colleague or gathering medical material in this course.

inThisLesson: Use the relevant process and information limits.
lessons.keyStatement: A broad design improvement and an individual request may both need attention.

flashcards.back: Usable access to a material, environment, service or method; its requirements depend on the setting.
An individual adjustment under the authorized process for a qualified applicant or employee with a disability.
A covered communication responsibility assessed for the task, context and person’s method.
The agency role responsible for appropriate coordination and medical-information requests under the employment policy.

items.title: Material barrier
items.body: A document problem can affect more than one person. Describe the failed task and seek an authorized review of the material. Do not require an employee to disclose a diagnosis before investigating a general inaccessible file.

items.title: Individual request
items.body: An employee’s request may need a different response even after a general document repair. Use the proper request procedure rather than infer that the employee is asking for a favor or needs to say a particular legal phrase. Do not promise a specific outcome before authorized review.

items.title: Communication method
items.body: A person who does not use sign language will not automatically benefit from a sign-language interpreter. Ask about the communication task and method through the applicable process. The useful assistance must fit the exchange, not a stereotype about a disability group.

tabs.heading: Two settings and one mistaken shortcut

tabs.label: Public-service material
tabs.body: A packet’s usability and communication needs are part of service access. Apply the relevant requirements and responsible review. Do not assume the employment request procedure is the only way a public participant can raise an access concern.

tabs.label: Employment request
tabs.body: Policy 1433 supplies the workplace accommodation process. Prompt routing and information limits matter even if the team is already improving materials for everyone. A general repair should not become a reason to ignore an individual request.

tabs.label: One solution for everyone
tabs.body: One format or aid may help some people and miss others. An accessible document is valuable but may not resolve a live communication task. Check the context and individual method, then use the appropriate authorized response.

check.question: What should staff do with the two practice concerns?
check.correct: Address the material barrier through its relevant access review and route the employee request under the employment procedure, preserving information limits.
wrong: Treat the document repair as automatic completion of the accommodation request.
Ask the employee’s supervisor to collect medical documentation.
Assign one communication aid to everyone with the same disability label.
check.feedbackCorrect: The response keeps the connected concerns distinct and preserves the responsible processes.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A general repair cannot establish that an individual request is resolved. Supervisors and managers also cannot request medical documentation under Policy 1433. Identify the setting, task and appropriate route without a group-based aid assignment.

items.text: Can the meeting packet be used in the relevant screen-reader task?
Which aid fits the covered public-service communication?
Who is the appropriate decision maker for the employee request?
Was the request promptly forwarded through the proper route?
A supervisor should collect the employee’s medical documentation.
One general repair completes every individual request.

lessons.next: Next, connect intercultural learning and antiracism to specific practices.

scenario.context: DHS practice case: A general packet repair is complete, and the team wants to ignore an employee’s separate request for a training adjustment.
options: Preserve the individual employment process and examine the separate request.
Require the employee to prove a diagnosis to the supervisor.
Declare one repaired packet meets every need.
responses: The general repair and individual request can require different actions.
Appropriate medical-information handling belongs to the authorized process, not supervisor collection.
The claim exceeds what the document repair establishes.

lessons.transfer: Map the two practice issues to their setting, task, appropriate route and information limit.

move.control: You can identify the issue and use the relevant response process.
move.failure: Related access concerns are collapsed into one route or a universal aid assumption.
move.next: Distinguish material access from an employment request before recommending a next step.

lessons.title: Connect intercultural learning and antiracism to practice
lessons.summary: Explain the terms without using identity as a diagnosis of an individual.
lessons.objective: Distinguish awareness of cultural differences from perspective shift and adapted practice.
objectives: Distinguish awareness of cultural differences from perspective shift and adapted practice.
Identify a racialized barrier question without assigning personal motive.
Explain why learning activity cannot determine a colleague’s intercultural orientation.
takeaways: Intercultural learning attends to culturally learned perspectives, differences and commonalities.
Antiracism examines and addresses racialized barriers rather than relying on good intention alone.
Do not infer an individual orientation or motive from identity or course participation.
lessons.statement: Use the terms to examine assumptions and practices, rather than label colleagues.

image.caption: Two colleagues point to a line in a printed document they are reviewing together.

intro.heading: Knowledge needs a connection to the work
intro.body:
Cultural awareness can begin with recognizing that people learn different assumptions about communication, authority, time or participation. Intercultural competence involves shifting cultural perspective and appropriately adapting behavior across culturally learned differences and commonalities. Learning a fact about a group or showing empathy does not, by itself, establish that a person has made that shift.

In the practice meeting, staff assume that useful disagreement must be immediate and public. A colleague explains that an appropriate written response after reflection can communicate a concern clearly. The team should check the actual task and perspectives rather than assign a national or racial group a fixed communication style. If culturally learned expectations are involved, examining them can help staff adapt the participation process while preserving the work’s purpose. Different methods can also arise from access, role or preparation conditions that are not cultural; do not force every difference into a cultural explanation.

Antiracism concerns intentional examination and action addressing racialized practices and barriers. A staff member can ask whether a selection or invitation process disadvantages a racialized community, which evidence supports the concern and which authorized change could address it. That inquiry is not a diagnosis that a named colleague has a particular motive, and one disparity measure alone does not establish the cause.

The official Intercultural Development Continuum describes orientations toward cultural differences and commonalities. These lessons do not assess or infer anyone’s orientation, convert participation into an IDI score or make an individual label part of an employee record. Use the concepts to reflect on assumptions and practice. A clearer contribution route or a supported barrier inquiry is evidence of a specific action, not proof that a person or organization has reached an assessed stage.

inThisLesson: Check whether the difference is culturally learned.
lessons.keyStatement: The question is how perspectives inform practice, not which label belongs to a person.

flashcards.back: Recognizing that culturally learned perspectives and assumptions can differ.
The capability to shift cultural perspective and appropriately adapt behavior across differences and commonalities.
Intentional examination and action addressing racialized practices and barriers.
This learning does not infer, score or record a person’s intercultural orientation.

items.title: Cultural and other conditions
items.body: A written response may reflect cultural expectations, preparation, access or an assigned work role. Ask about the specific conditions. Treating every method difference as a cultural trait can obscure the real issue and introduce a stereotype.

items.title: Adapted practice
items.body: If the task permits a written contribution route, changing the process can be a useful work action. It is intercultural adaptation only to the extent that culturally learned perspectives are understood and behavior appropriately shifts. A general accessibility repair alone does not establish an assessed orientation.

items.title: Racialized barriers
items.body: A process inquiry should specify the decision, affected opportunity and supporting evidence. Examine the practice and consequences without requiring a colleague to disclose personal beliefs or using identity as proof of motive. Formal discrimination concerns retain their applicable reporting routes.

tabs.label: Learned fact
tabs.body: A fact can add knowledge but does not show how staff respond to a culturally different perspective. Use the knowledge carefully and avoid expecting an individual to match a group description.

tabs.label: Adapted contribution process
tabs.body: A route informed by the relevant perspectives can change how knowledge reaches a decision. Describe the specific change and its limits. It cannot become a personal orientation score or a guarantee that every barrier is resolved.

tabs.label: Identity diagnosis
tabs.body: An identity-based explanation of a colleague’s motive or orientation skips evidence and formal assessment boundaries. Return to the actual practice, the culturally learned assumption where supported and the responsible next question.

check.question: What can the new written-response route establish?
check.correct: A specific participation change informed by the review; it does not diagnose a person’s orientation or settle every barrier.
wrong: Every staff member has reached Adaptation.
Every written preference comes from national culture.
Course participation is a valid individual IDI score.
check.feedbackCorrect: The statement recognizes a concrete change and keeps cultural interpretation and personal assessment appropriately bounded.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A route change cannot supply a formal personal assessment or explain every method preference. Check culturally learned perspectives where relevant and describe the work action, without assigning identity-based motives or orientations.

items.text: Intercultural competence involves perspective shift and appropriate behavior.
Antiracism includes examining racialized practices and barriers.
Which assumption prevents a usable contribution route?
What evidence supports the concern about access to an opportunity?
A quiet colleague must be at Minimization.
A person’s racial identity establishes their motive.

lessons.next: Finally, translate terminology into a clear work question and next step.

scenario.context: DHS practice case: The team offers a written contribution route and wants to record every employee as having advanced to an IDI orientation.
scenario.prompt: What should the record describe instead?
options: The specific process change and evidence, without individual orientation labels.
A hidden orientation score based on who used the route.
A cultural diagnosis of anyone who prefers the original method.
responses: The work result is useful without an unauthorized personal assessment.
Use of a route is not an IDI assessment and cannot become personnel labeling.
A preference does not establish a cultural diagnosis.

lessons.transfer: Explain one culturally learned assumption, one possible practice response and the limit on personal conclusions.

move.control: You can examine a relevant assumption and describe a specific action.
move.failure: Professional concepts become identity labels or inferred assessments.
move.next: Write a bounded explanation of the practice participation change.

lessons.title: Turn terminology into a clear question and follow-through
lessons.summary: Write a plain-language account of a specific DEIA concern.
lessons.objective: Rewrite an abstract DEIA statement into a task-specific question.
objectives: Rewrite an abstract DEIA statement into a task-specific question.
Identify evidence, authority and a responsible next step.
Distinguish a learning result from compliance or outcome certification.
takeaways: Explain the task, concern and supporting account.
Use required terms accurately and explain them when needed.
A course exercise supports preparation without certifying actual duties or results.
lessons.statement: Clear language should preserve substance and make the next step easier to understand.

image.caption: Two colleagues point to a line in a printed document they are reviewing together.

intro.heading: Say what needs to happen
intro.body:
Knowing terms is useful when staff can explain a concern and act appropriately. Replace an abstract statement with a concrete account of the task, the possible barrier, the supporting evidence and the next responsible step. Keep the relevant formal term if it names a real requirement, and explain it rather than substituting a vague promise.

For the practice meeting, “strengthen inclusion” could become “provide the relevant appendix before the review and ensure written questions reach the person deciding while the choice remains open.” That statement identifies a participation condition and an action. It still needs an authority and timing check, and it does not establish that every participant feels included. Another concern about an inaccessible document needs its own appropriate access review.

A plain-language account can also preserve uncertainty: one participant identified a navigation issue; the available test describes a particular task; further appropriate review is needed. This is more useful than claiming the meeting is fully equitable because a checklist was completed. Record how input informed a changed or unchanged choice, the reason and any question requiring another responsible office.

For actual work, follow required equity analysis and other applicable procedures. A glossary, preparation note or completed learning course does not replace those responsibilities or automatically supply required training credit. Consultant guidance can help staff build their own capability without becoming a universal approval gate. Practice with the practice meeting or a suitable draft within your role, keeping protected information out of learning activities. A clear question, supported account and responsible next step show useful learning even when an actual decision has not been completed.

lessons.keyStatement: Plain language makes the substance usable without removing its responsibilities.

flashcards.back: A clear description of the task, issue, evidence, limit and next step.
An action assigned to the role or office with appropriate authority.
Work that helps frame an analysis but does not establish that all required procedures are complete.
A conclusion about a result that needs appropriate evidence beyond course or activity completion.

accordion.heading: Write an account someone can use

items.title: Task and issue
items.body: Name the meeting packet, contribution route or other concrete task. Avoid saying only that the process needs more equity. A specific account helps a colleague understand what evidence to examine and which part of the process may need attention.

items.title: Evidence and limit
items.body: Explain what is known and what remains unresolved. A question arriving before finalization can show use of a route; it cannot establish everyone’s experience. Make that boundary clear without dismissing the contribution.

items.title: Action and authority
items.body: Identify who can review or change the task. Consultant guidance may support the analysis, while an access, employment or policy matter requires its own process. A clear next step should not invent authority or guarantee a decision.

tabs.label: Abstract promise
tabs.body: A promise of inclusion or equity expresses purpose but may leave staff unsure what to do. Keep the purpose and add the task, evidence question and responsibility. The explanation should guide action rather than display vocabulary.

tabs.label: Bounded work note
tabs.body: A bounded note says what happened, what it may affect and which review is needed. It can be useful before every question is settled. Preserve privacy and authority limits when using actual work information.

tabs.label: Certification claim
tabs.body: A statement that all obligations are met because terms were defined exceeds the exercise. Recognize the actual requirement and responsible process instead. Learning completion and operational results are different evidence.

check.question: Which final note is most useful?
check.correct: The appendix arrived late, written questions missed the decision, and the team will review timing and the contribution route within its authority.
wrong: All DEIA duties are complete because the glossary was read.
The varied attendance list guarantees belonging.
The consultant must approve every ordinary staff question.
check.feedbackCorrect: The note names a checkable task and responsible review without making a universal claim or an approval gate.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Glossary completion, attendance and consultant involvement cannot establish all duties or experiences. State the concrete concern, evidence, limit and relevant next responsibility in clear language.

items.text: The appendix reached the second unit after the decision closed.
A participant identified a specific navigation problem.
Check the contribution timeline with the authorized review owner.
Use the relevant access or employment process for the distinct concern.
Reading the glossary completes the required equity analysis.
One meeting repair proves everyone belongs.

lessons.next: Use the job aid to explain the relevant term, ask a concrete question and connect the concern to evidence and appropriate responsibility.

scenario.context: DHS practice case: A team has defined DEIA terms and now wants to publish a statement that every requirement and outcome is complete.
options: A bounded account of learning, the specific process concern and the responsible reviews still needed.
A more technical certification with no additional evidence.
No account at all because uncertainty remains.
responses: This recognizes real learning and keeps operational responsibilities visible.
Technical language cannot supply missing evidence or authority.
A clear account can be useful while its limits remain explicit.

lessons.transfer: Write a plain-language note with task, term, evidence, limit, responsible next step and review question.

move.control: You can make a substantive concern clear and usable.
move.failure: Terminology completion is mistaken for a complete policy analysis or result.
move.next: Use the practice meeting to write one clear question and a responsible next step.

jobAid.subtitle: Use the term to clarify the task, evidence and next responsibility.
remember: Representation, participation and belonging are related but different questions.
A recorded difference is not its own explanation or an automatic inequity finding.
General access and individual employment requests may require distinct responses.

sections.heading: Explain the meaning
items: Name the task and relevant term.
Ask what part of the process the concern describes.
Invite clarification without judging commitment or motive.

sections.heading: Examine evidence
items: Separate presence from influence, and an observation from its cause.
Ask about the specific task without compulsory identity or personal-history disclosure.
Record how input informed a changed or unchanged choice and the reasons.

sections.heading: Use appropriate responsibility
items: Distinguish public-service access from the employment accommodation process.
Do not infer or record a colleague’s intercultural orientation.
Use the actual required policy or access procedure; optional guidance supports staff capability.

sections.heading: Communicate the result
items: State what the record supports and what it cannot establish.
Identify the responsible next step and review question.
Do not treat a glossary or course completion as compliance or universal outcome certification.

sources.title: DHS — Equity Policy
sources.note: Primary DHS definitions of diversity, inclusion, equity, inequities, access and intercultural competence; formal policy duties remain distinct from these learning activities.

sources.title: MMB — ADA Reasonable Accommodation Policy 1433
sources.note: Employment accommodation has an individual authorized process. Supervisors and managers do not request medical information or documentation; an appropriate request belongs to the ADA Coordinator.

sources.title: U.S. Department of Justice — Effective Communication
sources.note: Primary guidance about communication disabilities, context and the person’s method. General accessibility planning does not establish that every individual communication need is met.

sources.title: IDI — Intercultural Development Continuum
sources.note: Official description of orientations toward culturally learned differences and commonalities. This course does not assess, infer or record an individual orientation.
